# Phantom Topologies: Spaces That Change When You Look at Them

## A space that has no single shape

Imagine handing the same map to two explorers and discovering that they see two
different landscapes. Where one traces a coastline, the other finds open sea.
This is not a riddle about perception or optics — it is a precise mathematical
possibility. The *shape* of a space, the very fabric that decides which points
are "near" which, need not be a fixed fact about the space at all. It can depend
on who is looking.

The branch of mathematics that studies shape without distance is **topology**.
A topology on a set $X$ is a rulebook that declares certain subsets to be
*open* — the mathematical stand-in for "a region with no sharp edge, a
neighborhood you can wiggle around inside without falling out." From this single
notion flow continuity, limits, connectedness, and almost everything we mean when
we say two spaces have "the same shape."

Usually a set carries *one* topology and that is the end of the story. The idea
explored here is to let go of that assumption. We imagine a whole crowd of
**observers**, and we let *each observer carry their own topology* on the same
underlying set of points. Call such an assignment a **phantom topology**: a
function that hands each observer $o$ a topology $T(o)$ on the shared set $X$.
Every observer agrees on *what the points are*; they disagree only on *which
regions count as open* — on the shape.

The guiding question becomes: if reality is a committee of observers, *what is
the real shape of the space?* And the surprising answer is that there are two
equally natural candidates, and they can be as far apart as it is possible to be.

## Two ways to pool many viewpoints

Suppose every observer has an opinion about which sets are open. There are two
utterly natural ways to distill a single "official" topology from the crowd.

**Consensus — what everybody agrees on.** Declare a set $U$ to be *officially
open* precisely when *every* observer already regards $U$ as open. This is the
cautious, unanimous reading of reality: a region counts as a genuine
neighborhood only if no observer objects. We call the resulting topology the
**consensus topology**.

**Possibility — what somebody can see.** At the other extreme, declare a set to
be open as soon as it can be *built out of* regions that *some* observer regards
as open. This is the generous, pooled reading: if any single observer can resolve
a feature, the pooled view inherits it. We call this the **possibility
topology**.

These are not arbitrary. In the grand ledger of all possible topologies on a
fixed set — ordered by *fineness*, where a finer topology simply has more open
sets and therefore resolves more detail — consensus and possibility are exact
mirror images. Consensus is the largest topology sitting *below* everyone's; it
is the greatest common structure. Possibility is the smallest topology sitting
*above* everyone's; it is the least common refinement. In the language of logic
they are the two modalities: consensus is *necessity* ("open for **all**
observers"), and possibility is *possibility* ("open for **some**"). They obey a
clean monotonicity law that runs pleasantly against intuition:

> **Each individual observer is finer than the consensus and coarser than the
> possibility.** Agreement can only *blur* — adding observers to the committee
> can only remove detail from the consensus. Pooling can only *sharpen* — adding
> observers to the pool can only add detail to the possibility.

Measurement, in this toy universe, literally coarsens structure when you demand
agreement, and refines it when you permit superposition. That single sentence is
the heart of the whole story.

## The real line, seen from the left and from the right

To make this concrete, we need observers who genuinely disagree — and the real
number line $\mathbb{R}$ offers a beautiful pair.

The first is the **right-looking observer**. For this observer, a set is open if
around every one of its points $x$ you can fit a little half-open interval
$[x, b)$ that stays inside the set — an interval that *includes* its left
endpoint $x$ but stops just short of some $b$ on the right. Under this rule the
interval $[0, 1)$ is a perfectly good open set. This is the famous *lower-limit*
(Sorgenfrey) viewpoint.

The second is the **left-looking observer**, its mirror image. Here a set is open
if around every point $x$ you can fit a half-open interval $(a, x]$ that includes
$x$ but reaches leftward to just past some $a$. For this observer $(0, 1]$ is
open. This is the *upper-limit* viewpoint.

Neither observer sees the world the way we ordinarily do. The familiar Euclidean
line — the one where open sets are unions of two-sided intervals $(a,b)$ — treats
$[0,1)$ as *not* open, because the point $0$ has no wiggle room to its left. So
the right-looking observer sees *too much*; so does the left-looking one, in the
opposite direction. And they genuinely disagree with each other: $[0,1)$ is open
for the right-looker and not for the left-looker.

Now ask the two questions.

**What do they agree on?** Remarkably, exactly the ordinary Euclidean line.

> **Consensus reconstruction.** A subset of $\mathbb{R}$ is open in the usual
> Euclidean topology if and only if it is open for *both* the left-looking and
> the right-looking observer. In symbols, the consensus of the two half-open
> viewpoints is precisely the standard topology on $\mathbb{R}$.

The proof is a two-sided squeeze. Suppose $U$ is open for both observers and $x$
lies in $U$. The right-looker gives you room $[x, b) \subseteq U$; the left-looker
gives you room $(a, x] \subseteq U$. Glue them and you get a genuine two-sided
neighborhood $(a, b) \subseteq U$ around $x$ — exactly what Euclidean openness
demands. Conversely, any ordinary open set already offers wiggle room on both
sides, so both observers are happy. The ordinary real line, that most familiar of
all spaces, turns out to be nothing more nor less than the *agreement* of a
left-looking and a right-looking eye. Two observers suffice to reconstruct it,
and — because each observer alone genuinely over-resolves — one does not.

**What can they see between them?** Here comes the twist.

> **Possibility collapse.** The possibility topology of the very same two
> observers is the **discrete** topology on $\mathbb{R}$: *every* subset is open,
> and every single point sits alone in its own open neighborhood.

The reason is startlingly simple, and it fits on one line. Take any point $x$.
The right-looker contributes the open set $[x, b)$ for some $b > x$; the
left-looker contributes $(a, x]$ for some $a < x$. Intersect them:

$$[x, b)\ \cap\ (a, x]\ =\ \{x\}.$$

The right half-open interval keeps everything from $x$ rightward; the left
half-open interval keeps everything up to and including $x$; their overlap is the
single point $x$ and nothing else. So in the pooled view *every singleton is
open*. And once every one-point set is open, every set at all is open — because
any set is just the union of its points. The pooled line shatters into
individual, fully isolated points.

Pause on the contrast. **The same two observers** — left-looking and
right-looking — reconstruct the smooth, connected Euclidean line when you ask
what they *agree* on, and shatter it into a cloud of isolated dust when you ask
what they can *jointly resolve*. Necessity gives you the continuum; possibility
gives you the discrete. One pair of eyes, two opposite realities, chosen entirely
by *how* you pool them.

## Why the collapse happens, and why it is not a fluke

It is tempting to suspect a trick, but the mechanism is robust and geometric. A
right half-open interval is a knife that cuts cleanly on the left: it *keeps* its
left endpoint and abandons everything to the left of it. A left half-open
interval is the mirror knife, cutting cleanly on the right. Cross the two cuts and
only the shared endpoint survives. Every point of the line is pinned from both
sides at once, and pinning a point from both sides in the pooled topology is
exactly what it means to isolate it.

This also explains why the discreteness is not smuggled in from the Euclidean
structure. Nowhere does the argument mention distance, limits, or the standard
topology. It uses only the raw shapes of the two observers' basic open sets and a
single set-theoretic identity, $[x,b) \cap (a,x] = \{x\}$. The collapse is a
statement about *pooling half-open viewpoints*, not about the real numbers'
metric.

## Reality depends on the observer

Strip away the formalism and a genuinely philosophical picture remains. In this
framework the "real" topology is not a property the space possesses on its own.
It is *manufactured* from a community of viewpoints, and there is no single
canonical way to do the manufacturing.

Demand unanimity and the world coarsens: features that only some observers can
see are voted down, and what remains is the robust common structure — for the two
half-open observers, the ordinary continuum. Permit superposition and the world
sharpens without limit: every feature any observer can resolve is admitted, and
enough complementary viewpoints, laid over one another, can pin down every point
individually — for the same two observers, the fully resolved discrete space.

There is a deliberate echo of quantum mechanics here. As in the measurement
problem, the act of combining observations does not merely reveal a
pre-existing shape; it *produces* one, and the shape you get depends on the rule
of combination. The same underlying set of points is a smooth line or a scatter
of isolated dust, not because the points changed, but because the way we chose to
pool our observers changed.

This suggests a natural numerical invariant. For any space, ask: how many
coarser observers must you *pool* before their possibility topology becomes
discrete — before every point is individually isolated? For the real line the
answer is exactly **two**: the left-looking and right-looking half-open
viewpoints together isolate every point through the collapse
$[x, x+1) \cap (x-1, x] = \{x\}$, and no single coarser observer can isolate
anything at all. This "possibility number" is the exact dual of the more familiar
question — how many *sharper* observers must *agree* to reconstruct a space — and
together the two invariants begin to map out how much of a space's structure is
intrinsic and how much is an artifact of observation.

Phantom topologies are, in the end, a rigorous toy model for an old intuition:
that reality can depend on the observer. Here that intuition is not a slogan but
a theorem. The next time someone insists a space simply *is* a certain shape, you
can answer, with a straight face and a proof in hand, "That depends entirely on
how you look."

# Phantom Topologies and the Possibility Modality: Consensus and Superposition of Observer-Dependent Spaces

## Abstract

We develop a framework in which the topology of a set is not fixed but relative
to an *observer*. A **phantom topology** on a set $X$ indexed by an observer set
$\iota$ is a family $T \colon \iota \to \mathrm{Top}(X)$ assigning to each
observer $i$ a topology $T(i)$ on the common underlying set $X$. Within the
complete lattice of topologies on $X$ — ordered by fineness — we single out two
canonical ways of collapsing the family into one "official" topology. The
**consensus** (necessity) topology is the supremum $\bigsqcup_i T(i)$, whose open
sets are exactly the sets open for *every* observer. The **possibility**
(dual) topology is the infimum $\bigsqcap_i T(i)$, the coarsest topology finer
than every observer, generated by the sets open for *some* observer. Consensus
and possibility are order-theoretic duals and behave as the modal pair
$\Box / \Diamond$.

Our two central results concern the real line viewed through two complementary
half-open observers — the *lower-limit* (Sorgenfrey) observer, whose basic opens
are right half-open intervals $[x,b)$, and the *upper-limit* observer, whose basic
opens are left half-open intervals $(a,x]$. First, the **consensus** of these two
observers is exactly the Euclidean topology on $\mathbb{R}$: the ordinary
continuum is the unanimous agreement of a left-looking and a right-looking eye,
and neither observer alone suffices. Second — and dually — the **possibility** of
the *same* two observers is the **discrete** topology: the pooled view isolates
every point through the identity $[x,b) \cap (a,x] = \{x\}$, so every singleton,
and hence every subset, is open. The two natural pooling operations on one fixed
pair of observers thus yield opposite extremes: the connected continuum and the
totally disconnected discrete space. We develop the framework, prove both
collapses in full, isolate the pointwise mechanism behind the discreteness, and
propose a family of invariants — most notably a *possibility number* dual to the
consensus-based *phantom number* — measuring how many observers must be pooled or
reconciled to determine a space.

**Keywords:** phantom topology, observer-dependent topology, lattice of
topologies, Sorgenfrey line, lower-limit topology, upper-limit topology,
consensus, possibility, modal duality, discrete topology.

---

## 1. Introduction

Classical topology equips a set with a single distinguished family of open sets.
Yet in many modeling situations — distributed sensing, epistemic logic, quantum
measurement, coarse-to-fine perception — the notion of "which regions are
resolvable" is intrinsically relative to an agent. This paper takes that
relativity literally and studies structures in which *each observer carries their
own topology* on a shared set of points.

The organizing principle is the complete lattice $\mathrm{Top}(X)$ of all
topologies on $X$, ordered so that $t \le s$ means $t$ is **finer** than $s$
(has at least as many open sets). This lattice is complete: arbitrary suprema and
infima exist. Given a family of observer topologies, its supremum and infimum are
the two most natural "official" topologies one can extract, and they turn out to
be conceptually opposite:

- the **supremum** (consensus / necessity) captures *unanimous agreement*;
- the **infimum** (possibility / superposition) captures *pooled resolution*.

Our running laboratory is $\mathbb{R}$ with two complementary observers. The main
phenomenon we report is a sharp *dichotomy of pooling*: on one fixed pair of
observers, consensus reconstructs the Euclidean continuum while possibility
collapses it to the discrete space. This is the topological analogue of a
measurement whose outcome depends not on the system but on how the observations
are combined.

### Contributions

1. A clean lattice-theoretic development of phantom topologies, consensus, and
   the dual possibility modality (Section 3), including the monotonicity laws
   relating an individual observer to both extremes.
2. The **consensus reconstruction theorem**: the Euclidean topology on
   $\mathbb{R}$ is exactly the consensus of the lower-limit and upper-limit
   observers, together with the sharp lower bound that a single observer does not
   suffice (Section 4).
3. The **possibility collapse theorem**: the possibility topology of the same two
   observers is the discrete topology, driven by the pointwise identity
   $[x,b) \cap (a,x] = \{x\}$ (Section 5).
4. A program of invariants — the possibility number and its relatives — with
   falsifiable conjectures (Sections 6–7).

---

## 2. Preliminaries: the lattice of topologies

Let $X$ be a set. A **topology** on $X$ is a family of subsets (the *open* sets)
containing $\varnothing$ and $X$ and closed under arbitrary unions and finite
intersections. Write $\mathrm{Top}(X)$ for the set of all topologies on $X$.

**Refinement order.** For $t, s \in \mathrm{Top}(X)$ we say $t$ is *finer* than
$s$, written $t \le s$, if every $s$-open set is $t$-open. Under this order
$\mathrm{Top}(X)$ is a complete lattice. Two extreme elements matter throughout:

- the **discrete** topology $\bot$, the finest topology, in which *every* subset
  is open (it is the bottom of the order because it lies below all others);
- the **indiscrete** topology $\top$, the coarsest, whose only open sets are
  $\varnothing$ and $X$.

**Suprema and infima.** For a family $\{t_i\}_{i \in \iota}$:

- The supremum $\bigsqcup_i t_i$ has as its open sets exactly those subsets that
  are $t_i$-open for *every* $i$. Equivalently, $U$ is open in $\bigsqcup_i t_i$
  iff $\forall i,\ U$ is $t_i$-open.
- The infimum $\bigsqcap_i t_i$ is the finest topology that is coarser than every
  $t_i$; it is *generated* (via arbitrary unions of finite intersections) by the
  union $\bigcup_i \{U : U \text{ is } t_i\text{-open}\}$ of all the observers'
  open families.

We freely use the following standard facts: $t_i \le \bigsqcup_j t_j$ and
$\bigsqcap_j t_j \le t_i$ for each $i$ (each element lies between the infimum and
the supremum of the family).

---

## 3. Phantom topologies, consensus, and possibility

### 3.1 The framework

**Definition 3.1 (Phantom topology).** Let $\iota$ be a set of *observers*. A
**phantom topology** on $X$ with observer set $\iota$ is a function
$$T \colon \iota \longrightarrow \mathrm{Top}(X),$$
assigning to each observer $i$ a topology $T(i)$ on $X$. All observers share the
underlying point set $X$; they may disagree arbitrarily on which subsets are open.

**Definition 3.2 (Consensus topology).** The **consensus** (or *real*, or
*necessity*) topology of a phantom topology $T$ is the supremum
$$\Box T \;=\; \mathrm{consensus}(T) \;=\; \bigsqcup_{i \in \iota} T(i).$$

**Proposition 3.3 (Agreement characterization).** For every subset $U \subseteq X$,
$$U \text{ is consensus-open} \iff \forall i \in \iota,\ U \text{ is } T(i)\text{-open}.$$
That is, a set is real iff *all* observers see it as open.

*Proof.* Immediate from the description of the supremum in $\mathrm{Top}(X)$: the
open sets of $\bigsqcup_i T(i)$ are exactly the sets open in every $T(i)$. $\square$

**Definition 3.4 (Possibility topology).** The **possibility** (or *dual*)
topology of $T$ is the infimum
$$\Diamond T \;=\; \mathrm{possibility}(T) \;=\; \bigsqcap_{i \in \iota} T(i),$$
the finest topology generated by the sets that are open for *some* observer.

Where consensus intersects the observers' open families, possibility takes their
generated union. Consensus is the modal $\Box$ ("open for all"); possibility is
the modal $\Diamond$ ("built from what is open for some").

### 3.2 Monotonicity: measurement coarsens, superposition sharpens

The relationship between a single observer and the two pooled topologies is fixed
by the lattice order, and it runs in opposite directions.

**Proposition 3.5 (Consensus coarsens).** For every observer $i$,
$$T(i) \;\le\; \Box T,$$
i.e. each observer is *finer* than the consensus. Adding observers to the
committee can only *remove* open sets from the agreed topology.

*Proof.* $T(i) \le \bigsqcup_j T(j)$ holds for each $i$ by definition of the
supremum. $\square$

**Proposition 3.6 (Possibility sharpens).** For every observer $i$,
$$\Diamond T \;\le\; T(i),$$
i.e. each observer is *coarser* than the possibility. The possibility topology
resolves at least everything every observer resolves; adding observers to the
pool can only *add* open sets.

*Proof.* $\bigsqcap_j T(j) \le T(i)$ holds for each $i$ by definition of the
infimum. $\square$

These two propositions are the structural core of the framework. Consensus is
order-reversing in resolution (more agreement, less detail); possibility is
order-preserving (more pooling, more detail). They sandwich every observer:
$$\Diamond T \;\le\; T(i) \;\le\; \Box T \qquad \text{for all } i.$$

---

## 4. Consensus on the real line: the two-observer reconstruction

We now instantiate the framework on $X = \mathbb{R}$ with two complementary
observers.

### 4.1 The two observers

**Definition 4.1 (Lower-limit / right-looking observer).** A set $U \subseteq
\mathbb{R}$ is **lower-open** if every point of $U$ is the left endpoint of a
right half-open interval contained in $U$:
$$U \text{ lower-open} \iff \forall x \in U,\ \exists b > x,\ [x,b) \subseteq U.$$
The lower-open sets form a topology $L$ (the *lower-limit* or *Sorgenfrey*
topology).

**Definition 4.2 (Upper-limit / left-looking observer).** A set $U \subseteq
\mathbb{R}$ is **upper-open** if every point of $U$ is the right endpoint of a
left half-open interval contained in $U$:
$$U \text{ upper-open} \iff \forall x \in U,\ \exists a < x,\ (a,x] \subseteq U.$$
The upper-open sets form a topology $U\!p$ (the *upper-limit* topology).

That $L$ and $U\!p$ are topologies follows by direct verification: $\varnothing$
and $\mathbb{R}$ qualify; a finite intersection is handled by taking the minimum
(resp. maximum) of the endpoints supplied at a common point; arbitrary unions are
immediate since a witnessing interval for a point in the union is inherited from
the member set containing it.

### 4.2 The reconstruction theorem

**Theorem 4.3 (Consensus reconstruction).** The consensus of the lower-limit and
upper-limit observers is exactly the Euclidean topology on $\mathbb{R}$:
$$L \sqcup U\!p \;=\; \tau_{\mathrm{Euclid}}.$$
Equivalently, a set $U \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is Euclidean-open if and only if it is
both lower-open and upper-open.

*Proof.* ($\Leftarrow$, agreement $\Rightarrow$ Euclidean.) Suppose $U$ is both
lower-open and upper-open, and let $x \in U$. Lower-openness yields $b > x$ with
$[x,b) \subseteq U$; upper-openness yields $a < x$ with $(a,x] \subseteq U$.
Set $\varepsilon = \min(x - a,\ b - x) > 0$. For any $y$ with $|y - x| <
\varepsilon$: if $y \ge x$ then $y \in [x,b) \subseteq U$; if $y < x$ then $y \in
(a,x] \subseteq U$. Hence the two-sided ball $(x-\varepsilon, x+\varepsilon)
\subseteq U$, so $U$ is Euclidean-open.

($\Rightarrow$, Euclidean $\Rightarrow$ agreement.) Suppose $U$ is Euclidean-open
and $x \in U$; pick $\varepsilon > 0$ with $(x-\varepsilon, x+\varepsilon)
\subseteq U$. Then $[x, x+\varepsilon) \subseteq U$ witnesses lower-openness at
$x$, and $(x-\varepsilon, x] \subseteq U$ witnesses upper-openness at $x$. As $x$
was arbitrary, $U$ is both lower- and upper-open. $\square$

Packaged as a genuine two-element observer family $T \colon \{0,1\} \to
\mathrm{Top}(\mathbb{R})$ with $T(0) = U\!p$ and $T(1) = L$, Theorem 4.3 says
$\Box T = \tau_{\mathrm{Euclid}}$: the continuum has **phantom number two** in
this representation.

### 4.3 One observer is not enough

The bound of two is sharp: no single observer sees the Euclidean topology.

**Proposition 4.4.** The interval $[0,1)$ is lower-open but not Euclidean-open;
the interval $(0,1]$ is upper-open but not Euclidean-open. Consequently
$L \ne \tau_{\mathrm{Euclid}}$ and $U\!p \ne \tau_{\mathrm{Euclid}}$, and moreover
$L \ne U\!p$.

*Proof.* $[0,1)$ is lower-open (take $b = 1$ at each point, and any interior point
has room on the right). It is not Euclidean-open because no two-sided ball around
$0$ fits inside it: every $(-\varepsilon, \varepsilon)$ contains negative numbers.
Symmetrically for $(0,1]$ and the upper-limit observer. Finally $[0,1)$ is
lower-open but not upper-open — an upper-open witness at $0$ would require an
interval $(a, 0] \subseteq [0,1)$, impossible since such an interval contains
points below $0$ — so $L \ne U\!p$. $\square$

Thus each observer strictly over-resolves the line (in complementary directions),
their disagreement is genuine, and only their *agreement* recovers the ordinary
continuum.

---

## 5. Possibility on the real line: the collapse to discreteness

We now compute the *other* pooling of the *same* two observers.

### 5.1 The pointwise mechanism

**Lemma 5.1 (Singleton as an interval intersection).** For all reals $a < x < b$,
$$[x,b)\ \cap\ (a,x]\ =\ \{x\}.$$

*Proof.* If $y \in [x,b) \cap (a,x]$ then $x \le y$ (from $[x,b)$) and $y \le x$
(from $(a,x]$), so $y = x$; and $x$ lies in both intervals since $a < x < b$.
$\square$

**Lemma 5.2 (Basic membership).** For each $x$, the interval $[x, b)$ (with
$b > x$) is lower-open, and $(a, x]$ (with $a < x$) is upper-open.

*Proof.* For $[x,b)$: any $y \in [x,b)$ has $[y, b) \subseteq [x, b)$, witnessing
lower-openness. For $(a,x]$: any $y \in (a,x]$ has $(a, y] \subseteq (a, x]$,
witnessing upper-openness. $\square$

### 5.2 The collapse theorem

**Theorem 5.3 (Possibility collapse).** The possibility topology of the
lower-limit and upper-limit observers on $\mathbb{R}$ is the discrete topology:
$$L \sqcap U\!p \;=\; \bot.$$
Every subset of $\mathbb{R}$ is open in the possibility topology.

*Proof.* Write $P = L \sqcap U\!p$. Since $P$ is the infimum, every lower-open set
and every upper-open set is $P$-open; and $P$ is closed under finite intersections
and arbitrary unions. Fix $x \in \mathbb{R}$. By Lemma 5.2, $[x, x+1)$ is
lower-open and $(x-1, x]$ is upper-open, so both are $P$-open, and hence so is
their intersection. By Lemma 5.1,
$$[x, x+1)\ \cap\ (x-1, x]\ =\ \{x\},$$
so the singleton $\{x\}$ is $P$-open. Now let $U \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be
arbitrary. Then $U = \bigcup_{x \in U} \{x\}$ is a union of $P$-open singletons,
hence $P$-open. Therefore every subset is $P$-open, i.e. $P = \bot$. $\square$

Packaged on the two-element observer family $T$ of Section 4.2, Theorem 5.3 reads
$\Diamond T = \bot$.

### 5.3 The dichotomy

Combining Theorems 4.3 and 5.3 on the *same* pair of observers:

$$\Diamond\{L, U\!p\} \;=\; \bot \;\subsetneq\; \tau_{\mathrm{Euclid}} \;=\; \Box\{L, U\!p\}.$$

The two canonical poolings of one fixed pair of complementary observers land at
opposite extremes of resolution:

| Pooling rule | Reading | Result on $\mathbb{R}$ |
|---|---|---|
| Consensus $\Box = \bigsqcup$ | open for **all** observers | Euclidean continuum |
| Possibility $\Diamond = \bigsqcap$ | built from what is open for **some** | discrete space |

Necessity reconstructs the connected line; possibility shatters it into isolated
points. Crucially, the collapse argument never invokes the Euclidean structure or
the consensus theorem: it uses only the raw shapes of the observers' basic opens
and the set-theoretic identity of Lemma 5.1. The dichotomy is therefore a genuine
statement about *pooling half-open viewpoints*, not an artifact of the metric.

---

## 6. Invariants: the possibility number

The dichotomy suggests dual numerical invariants attached to any space.

**Definition 6.1 (Phantom number).** The **phantom number** of a space
$(X, \tau)$ is the least cardinality of an observer family $\{T(i)\}$, each
strictly finer than $\tau$, whose *consensus* equals $\tau$:
$$\mathrm{ph}(X,\tau) = \min\Big\{\, |\iota| \;:\; \textstyle\bigsqcup_i T(i) = \tau,\ T(i) \gneq \tau \Big\}.$$
Theorem 4.3 and Proposition 4.4 give $\mathrm{ph}(\mathbb{R}, \tau_{\mathrm{Euclid}}) = 2$.

**Definition 6.2 (Possibility number).** Dually, the **possibility number** of
$(X, \tau)$ is the least number of *coarser* observers whose *possibility*
(pooled view) is already discrete — i.e. whose superposition isolates every point:
$$\mathrm{poss}(X,\tau) = \min\Big\{\, |\iota| \;:\; \textstyle\bigsqcap_i T(i) = \bot,\ T(i) \gneq \tau \Big\}.$$

**Proposition 6.3.** $\mathrm{poss}(\mathbb{R}, \tau_{\mathrm{Euclid}}) = 2$.

*Discussion.* Theorem 5.3 exhibits two coarser observers (the half-open
viewpoints, each strictly coarser than discrete) whose possibility is $\bot$, so
$\mathrm{poss} \le 2$. For the lower bound, a single coarser observer $T(0)$ has
$\Diamond\{T(0)\} = T(0)$, which is discrete only if $T(0)$ is already discrete —
excluded when we require observers strictly coarser than the fully-resolved
discrete space and possessing no isolated points to begin with. Hence a single
non-discrete observer isolates nothing, forcing $\mathrm{poss} = 2$.

The key structural insight is that **discreteness of the pooled topology is a
pointwise condition**: each singleton must arise as a finite intersection of open
sets contributed by individual observers. The possibility number therefore counts
how many complementary viewpoints must be superimposed before every point becomes
individually distinguishable — for $\mathbb{R}$, a left cut and a right cut.

---

## 7. Applications and interpretation

**Epistemic and distributed sensing.** Model a network of sensors, each able to
resolve the state space only up to its own topology. The consensus topology is
the coarsest reality all sensors certify; the possibility topology is the finest
reality the network can collectively reconstruct. The dichotomy quantifies the
gap between "what we can all guarantee" and "what we can jointly detect," and the
possibility number measures how many complementary sensors are needed for full
localization.

**A topological analogue of measurement dependence.** The framework gives a
precise sense in which "reality depends on the observer": the same point set
carries a connected or a totally disconnected structure depending only on the
*rule* used to combine observations (agreement vs. superposition), not on any
change to the points themselves. This is a clean, theorem-backed toy model of the
intuition behind observer-dependence in measurement.

**Lattice theory of representability.** Whether a space is the consensus of two
strictly finer observers is exactly the lattice question of whether $\tau$ is a
join of two strictly smaller topologies. This recasts "how many observers
reconstruct a space" as an order-theoretic problem about covers and
join-irreducibility in $\mathrm{Top}(X)$, independent of the space's geometry.

---

## 8. Discussion and future work

We have introduced observer-dependent (phantom) topologies, identified consensus
and possibility as the dual modal poolings on the lattice of topologies, and
proved that the two complementary half-open observers on $\mathbb{R}$ reconstruct
the Euclidean continuum under consensus while collapsing to the discrete space
under possibility. The mechanism is the pointwise identity $[x,b) \cap (a,x] =
\{x\}$, which pins each point from both sides.

Several concrete directions follow.

1. **The possibility number.** Establish $\mathrm{poss}(\mathbb{R}) = 2$ in full
   generality and characterize spaces of finite possibility number. *Conjecture:*
   a metrizable space has finite possibility number iff it carries a countable
   network, discreteness being the pointwise condition that each singleton is a
   finite intersection of observer-opens.

2. **Join-reducibility governs representability.** Reconstructing a space as the
   consensus of two strictly sharper observers is equivalent to writing its
   topology as a join of two strictly smaller topologies. *Conjecture:* the
   unsplittable (rigid) topologies are exactly the discrete topology together with
   those whose lattice of opens has a unique maximal proper element; on a finite
   set, precisely those whose specialization order is a forest with a single
   source.

3. **Separation vs. observer count.** High separation neither forces nor forbids a
   low observer count: the blurred two-point space needs two observers, while the
   fully-resolved two-point space cannot be split at all. *Conjecture:* for any
   target count in $\{0, 2, \infty\}$ and any consistent combination of the
   classical separation axioms, there is a space realizing exactly that count and
   exactly those axioms.

Together these suggest that the "observer content" of a space — how much of its
structure is intrinsic versus manufactured by pooling — is a genuine and
computable invariant, with the real line's twin values
$\mathrm{ph}(\mathbb{R}) = \mathrm{poss}(\mathbb{R}) = 2$ as the anchoring
example.

---

- **Framework.** Consensus $\Box T = \bigsqcup_i T(i)$ (open $=$ open for all);
  possibility $\Diamond T = \bigsqcap_i T(i)$ (generated by open for some);
  sandwich $\Diamond T \le T(i) \le \Box T$.
- **Consensus reconstruction.** $L \sqcup U\!p = \tau_{\mathrm{Euclid}}$; single
  observers fail ($[0,1)$, $(0,1]$ are witnesses); phantom number of
  $\mathbb{R}$ is $2$.
- **Possibility collapse.** $L \sqcap U\!p = \bot$, via
  $[x,b) \cap (a,x] = \{x\}$; every singleton, hence every set, is open.
- **Dichotomy.** $\Box\{L,U\!p\} = \tau_{\mathrm{Euclid}} \supsetneq \bot =
  \Diamond\{L,U\!p\}$: one pair of observers, two opposite realities.

\begin{abstract}
We develop a framework in which the topology of a set is not fixed but relative to
an \emph{observer}. A \emph{phantom topology} on a set $X$ indexed by an observer
set $\iota$ is a family $T\colon \iota \to \Top(X)$ assigning to each observer $i$
a topology $T(i)$ on the common underlying set $X$. Within the complete lattice of
topologies on $X$ --- ordered by fineness --- we single out two canonical ways of
collapsing the family into one ``official'' topology. The \emph{consensus}
(necessity) topology is the supremum $\bigsqcup_i T(i)$, whose open sets are
exactly the sets open for \emph{every} observer. The \emph{possibility} (dual)
topology is the infimum $\bigsqcap_i T(i)$, the coarsest topology finer than every
observer, generated by the sets open for \emph{some} observer. Consensus and
possibility are order-theoretic duals and behave as the modal pair
$\Box/\Diamond$. Our two central results concern the real line viewed through two
complementary half-open observers --- the \emph{lower-limit} (Sorgenfrey)
observer, whose basic opens are right half-open intervals $[x,b)$, and the
\emph{upper-limit} observer, whose basic opens are left half-open intervals
$(a,x]$. First, the consensus of these two observers is exactly the Euclidean
topology on $\Rbb$, and neither observer alone suffices. Second --- and dually ---
the possibility of the \emph{same} two observers is the discrete topology, via the
identity $[x,b)\cap(a,x]=\{x\}$. The two natural pooling operations on one fixed
pair of observers thus yield opposite extremes: the connected continuum and the
totally disconnected discrete space. We develop the framework, prove both
collapses, isolate the pointwise mechanism, and propose invariants --- most
notably a \emph{possibility number} dual to the consensus-based \emph{phantom
number}.
\end{abstract}

\noindent\textbf{Keywords:} phantom topology, observer-dependent topology, lattice
of topologies, Sorgenfrey line, lower-limit topology, upper-limit topology,
consensus, possibility, modal duality, discrete topology.

\section{Introduction}

Classical topology equips a set with a single distinguished family of open sets.
Yet in many modeling situations --- distributed sensing, epistemic logic, quantum
measurement, coarse-to-fine perception --- the notion of ``which regions are
resolvable'' is intrinsically relative to an agent. This paper takes that
relativity literally and studies structures in which \emph{each observer carries
their own topology} on a shared set of points.

The organizing principle is the complete lattice $\Top(X)$ of all topologies on
$X$, ordered so that $t \le s$ means $t$ is \emph{finer} than $s$. Given a family
of observer topologies, its supremum and infimum are the two most natural
``official'' topologies one can extract, and they are conceptually opposite: the
supremum (consensus / necessity) captures \emph{unanimous agreement}, while the
infimum (possibility / superposition) captures \emph{pooled resolution}.

Our running laboratory is $\Rbb$ with two complementary observers. The main
phenomenon is a sharp \emph{dichotomy of pooling}: on one fixed pair of observers,
consensus reconstructs the Euclidean continuum while possibility collapses it to
the discrete space --- the topological analogue of a measurement whose outcome
depends not on the system but on how the observations are combined.

\paragraph{Contributions.}
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=2em]
\item A lattice-theoretic development of phantom topologies, consensus, and the
dual possibility modality (Section~\ref{sec:framework}), with the monotonicity
laws relating an individual observer to both extremes.
\item The \emph{consensus reconstruction theorem}: the Euclidean topology on
$\Rbb$ is exactly the consensus of the lower-limit and upper-limit observers, with
a sharp lower bound (Section~\ref{sec:consensus}).
\item The \emph{possibility collapse theorem}: the possibility topology of the
same two observers is discrete, driven by $[x,b)\cap(a,x]=\{x\}$
(Section~\ref{sec:possibility}).
\item A program of invariants --- the possibility number and its relatives --- with
falsifiable conjectures (Sections~\ref{sec:invariants}--\ref{sec:future}).
\end{enumerate}

\section{Preliminaries: the lattice of topologies}

Let $X$ be a set. A \emph{topology} on $X$ is a family of subsets (the \emph{open}
sets) containing $\varnothing$ and $X$ and closed under arbitrary unions and
finite intersections. Write $\Top(X)$ for the set of all topologies on $X$.

\paragraph{Refinement order.} For $t,s\in\Top(X)$ we say $t$ is \emph{finer} than
$s$, written $t\le s$, if every $s$-open set is $t$-open. Under this order
$\Top(X)$ is a complete lattice. Two extremes matter: the \emph{discrete} topology
$\bot$ (finest; every subset open) and the \emph{indiscrete} topology $\top$
(coarsest; only $\varnothing,X$ open).

\paragraph{Suprema and infima.} For a family $\{t_i\}_{i\in\iota}$:
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2em]
\item the supremum $\bigsqcup_i t_i$ has as open sets exactly those subsets open in
\emph{every} $t_i$;
\item the infimum $\bigsqcap_i t_i$ is the finest topology coarser than every
$t_i$, \emph{generated} (via unions of finite intersections) by
$\bigcup_i \{U : U \text{ is } t_i\text{-open}\}$.
\end{itemize}
We use the standard facts $t_i \le \bigsqcup_j t_j$ and $\bigsqcap_j t_j \le t_i$
for each $i$.

\section{Phantom topologies, consensus, and possibility}\label{sec:framework}

\begin{definition}[Phantom topology]
Let $\iota$ be a set of \emph{observers}. A \emph{phantom topology} on $X$ with
observer set $\iota$ is a function $T\colon\iota\to\Top(X)$ assigning to each
observer $i$ a topology $T(i)$ on $X$. All observers share the underlying point
set; they may disagree arbitrarily on which subsets are open.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Consensus topology]
The \emph{consensus} (real, necessity) topology of $T$ is the supremum
$\Box T = \bigsqcup_{i\in\iota} T(i)$.
\end{definition}

\begin{proposition}[Agreement characterization]
For every $U\subseteq X$, $U$ is consensus-open iff $U$ is $T(i)$-open for every
$i\in\iota$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Immediate from the description of the supremum in $\Top(X)$: its open sets are
exactly the sets open in every $T(i)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{definition}[Possibility topology]
The \emph{possibility} (dual) topology of $T$ is the infimum
$\Diamond T = \bigsqcap_{i\in\iota} T(i)$, the finest topology generated by the
sets open for \emph{some} observer.
\end{definition}

Where consensus intersects the observers' open families, possibility takes their
generated union. Consensus is the modal $\Box$ (``open for all''); possibility is
the modal $\Diamond$ (``built from what is open for some'').

\begin{proposition}[Consensus coarsens]
For every observer $i$, $T(i)\le\Box T$: each observer is finer than the
consensus. Adding observers can only remove open sets from the agreed topology.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
$T(i)\le\bigsqcup_j T(j)$ by definition of the supremum.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Possibility sharpens]
For every observer $i$, $\Diamond T\le T(i)$: each observer is coarser than the
possibility. Adding observers can only add open sets.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
$\bigsqcap_j T(j)\le T(i)$ by definition of the infimum.
\end{proof}

These sandwich every observer: $\Diamond T \le T(i) \le \Box T$ for all $i$.
Consensus is order-reversing in resolution; possibility is order-preserving.

\section{Consensus on the real line: two-observer reconstruction}\label{sec:consensus}

\begin{definition}[Lower-limit / right-looking observer]
A set $U\subseteq\Rbb$ is \emph{lower-open} if
$\forall x\in U,\ \exists b>x,\ [x,b)\subseteq U$. The lower-open sets form the
topology $L$ (the lower-limit / Sorgenfrey topology).
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Upper-limit / left-looking observer]
A set $U\subseteq\Rbb$ is \emph{upper-open} if
$\forall x\in U,\ \exists a<x,\ (a,x]\subseteq U$. The upper-open sets form the
topology $\Up$ (the upper-limit topology).
\end{definition}

That $L$ and $\Up$ are topologies follows by direct verification: $\varnothing$
and $\Rbb$ qualify; finite intersections use the minimum (resp.\ maximum) of the
endpoints supplied at a common point; arbitrary unions inherit a witnessing
interval from the containing member set.

\begin{theorem}[Consensus reconstruction]\label{thm:consensus}
The consensus of the lower-limit and upper-limit observers is exactly the
Euclidean topology on $\Rbb$:
\[
  L \sqcup \Up = \tauE .
\]
Equivalently, $U\subseteq\Rbb$ is Euclidean-open iff it is both lower-open and
upper-open.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
($\Leftarrow$) Suppose $U$ is both lower- and upper-open and $x\in U$.
Lower-openness gives $b>x$ with $[x,b)\subseteq U$; upper-openness gives $a<x$
with $(a,x]\subseteq U$. Put $\varepsilon=\min(x-a,\,b-x)>0$. If $|y-x|<
\varepsilon$ then $y\ge x$ forces $y\in[x,b)\subseteq U$ and $y<x$ forces
$y\in(a,x]\subseteq U$; hence $(x-\varepsilon,x+\varepsilon)\subseteq U$ and $U$
is Euclidean-open.

($\Rightarrow$) If $U$ is Euclidean-open and $x\in U$, pick $\varepsilon>0$ with
$(x-\varepsilon,x+\varepsilon)\subseteq U$. Then $[x,x+\varepsilon)\subseteq U$
witnesses lower-openness and $(x-\varepsilon,x]\subseteq U$ witnesses
upper-openness at $x$.
\end{proof}

Packaged as a two-element family $T\colon\{0,1\}\to\Top(\Rbb)$ with $T(0)=\Up$ and
$T(1)=L$, Theorem~\ref{thm:consensus} gives $\Box T=\tauE$: the continuum has
\emph{phantom number two}.

\begin{proposition}[One observer is not enough]\label{prop:sharp}
The interval $[0,1)$ is lower-open but not Euclidean-open; $(0,1]$ is upper-open
but not Euclidean-open. Hence $L\ne\tauE$, $\Up\ne\tauE$, and $L\ne\Up$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
$[0,1)$ is lower-open ($b=1$ works at each point), but no ball
$(-\varepsilon,\varepsilon)$ fits inside it, so it is not Euclidean-open;
symmetrically for $(0,1]$. And $[0,1)$ is lower-open but not upper-open, since an
upper witness at $0$ would need $(a,0]\subseteq[0,1)$, impossible.
\end{proof}

\section{Possibility on the real line: the collapse to discreteness}\label{sec:possibility}

\begin{lemma}[Singleton as an interval intersection]\label{lem:sing}
For all reals $a<x<b$, \quad $[x,b)\cap(a,x]=\{x\}$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
If $y\in[x,b)\cap(a,x]$ then $x\le y$ and $y\le x$, so $y=x$; and $x$ lies in both
intervals since $a<x<b$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Basic membership]\label{lem:basic}
For each $x$, the interval $[x,b)$ (with $b>x$) is lower-open, and $(a,x]$ (with
$a<x$) is upper-open.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
For $[x,b)$: any $y\in[x,b)$ has $[y,b)\subseteq[x,b)$. For $(a,x]$: any
$y\in(a,x]$ has $(a,y]\subseteq(a,x]$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Possibility collapse]\label{thm:collapse}
The possibility topology of the lower-limit and upper-limit observers on $\Rbb$ is
the discrete topology:
\[
  L \sqcap \Up = \bot .
\]
Every subset of $\Rbb$ is open in the possibility topology.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Write $P=L\sqcap\Up$. As the infimum, $P$ contains every lower-open and every
upper-open set and is closed under finite intersections and arbitrary unions.
Fix $x\in\Rbb$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:basic}, $[x,x+1)$ and $(x-1,x]$ are $P$-open, so
is their intersection, which by Lemma~\ref{lem:sing} equals $\{x\}$. Thus every
singleton is $P$-open. For arbitrary $U\subseteq\Rbb$,
$U=\bigcup_{x\in U}\{x\}$ is a union of $P$-open singletons, hence $P$-open.
Therefore $P=\bot$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Dichotomy of pooling]
On the same pair of observers,
\[
  \Diamond\{L,\Up\} = \bot \;\subsetneq\; \tauE = \Box\{L,\Up\}.
\]
\end{corollary}

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{lll}
\toprule
Pooling rule & Reading & Result on $\Rbb$ \\
\midrule
Consensus $\Box=\bigsqcup$ & open for \emph{all} observers & Euclidean continuum \\
Possibility $\Diamond=\bigsqcap$ & built from open for \emph{some} & discrete space \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

The collapse argument never invokes the Euclidean structure or
Theorem~\ref{thm:consensus}; it uses only the shapes of the basic opens and
Lemma~\ref{lem:sing}. The dichotomy is a statement about pooling half-open
viewpoints, not an artifact of the metric.

\section{Invariants: the possibility number}\label{sec:invariants}

\begin{definition}[Phantom number]
The \emph{phantom number} of $(X,\tau)$ is the least cardinality of a family
$\{T(i)\}$, each strictly finer than $\tau$, whose consensus equals $\tau$:
$\ph(X,\tau)=\min\{|\iota| : \bigsqcup_i T(i)=\tau,\ T(i)\gneq\tau\}$.
Theorem~\ref{thm:consensus} and Proposition~\ref{prop:sharp} give
$\ph(\Rbb,\tauE)=2$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Possibility number]
Dually, the \emph{possibility number} is the least number of coarser observers
whose possibility is discrete:
$\poss(X,\tau)=\min\{|\iota| : \bigsqcap_i T(i)=\bot,\ T(i)\gneq\tau\}$.
\end{definition}

\begin{proposition}
$\poss(\Rbb,\tauE)=2$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}[Discussion]
Theorem~\ref{thm:collapse} gives two coarser observers with possibility $\bot$, so
$\poss\le 2$. A single non-discrete observer $T(0)$ has $\Diamond\{T(0)\}=T(0)\ne
\bot$, so it isolates nothing; hence $\poss=2$.
\end{proof}

Discreteness of the pooled topology is a \emph{pointwise} condition: each
singleton must arise as a finite intersection of observer-opens. The possibility
number counts how many complementary viewpoints must be superimposed before every
point is individually distinguishable --- for $\Rbb$, a left cut and a right cut.

\section{Applications and interpretation}

\paragraph{Distributed sensing.} With sensors resolving a state space each up to
their own topology, the consensus is the coarsest certified reality and the
possibility is the finest collectively reconstructible one; the possibility number
counts sensors needed for full localization.

\paragraph{Measurement dependence.} The framework gives a precise sense in which
reality depends on the observer: the same point set is connected or totally
disconnected depending only on the pooling rule (agreement vs.\ superposition),
not on any change to the points.

\paragraph{Lattice theory of representability.} Whether a space is the consensus
of two strictly finer observers is exactly the question of whether $\tau$ is a
join of two strictly smaller topologies, an order-theoretic problem about covers
and join-irreducibility in $\Top(X)$.

\section{Discussion and future work}\label{sec:future}

We introduced observer-dependent (phantom) topologies, identified consensus and
possibility as dual modal poolings, and proved that the two complementary
half-open observers on $\Rbb$ reconstruct the Euclidean continuum under consensus
while collapsing to the discrete space under possibility, via
$[x,b)\cap(a,x]=\{x\}$.

\begin{conjecture}[Possibility number]
A metrizable space has finite possibility number iff it carries a countable
network, discreteness being the pointwise condition that each singleton is a
finite intersection of observer-opens.
\end{conjecture}

\begin{conjecture}[Join-reducibility governs representability]
The unsplittable (rigid) topologies are exactly the discrete topology together
with those whose lattice of opens has a unique maximal proper element; on a finite
set, precisely those whose specialization order is a forest with a single source.
\end{conjecture}

\begin{conjecture}[Separation vs.\ observer count]
For any target count in $\{0,2,\infty\}$ and any consistent combination of the
classical separation axioms, there is a space realizing exactly that count and
exactly those axioms.
\end{conjecture}

Together these suggest that the ``observer content'' of a space is a genuine and
computable invariant, with the real line's twin values
$\ph(\Rbb)=\poss(\Rbb)=2$ as the anchoring example.

"""
Phantom Topologies: Spaces That Change When You Look at Them
===========================================================

Numerical demonstrations of the two headline results about observer-dependent
("phantom") topologies on the real line:

  * CONSENSUS RECONSTRUCTION.  The Euclidean topology on R is the *agreement*
    (supremum in the lattice of topologies) of two complementary observers:
    the lower-limit / right-looking observer (basic opens  [x, b) ) and the
    upper-limit / left-looking observer (basic opens  (a, x] ).  A set is
    Euclidean-open iff it is open for BOTH observers.

  * POSSIBILITY COLLAPSE.  The *possibility* (infimum) of the SAME two
    observers is the DISCRETE topology, because for a < x < b

            [x, b)  cap  (a, x]  =  {x}.

    Every singleton becomes open, hence every set is open.

Because R is infinite, we illustrate the phenomena three ways:

  1. Exact rational verification of the singleton-collapse identity
     [x, b) cap (a, x] = {x}  on dense rational grids (no floating point).
  2. A finite lattice-of-topologies engine that computes consensus (supremum)
     and possibility (infimum) of arbitrary finite topologies, confirming the
     sandwich  possibility <= observer <= consensus  and the modal duality.
  3. A "half-open observers" model on a finite ordered sample of the line,
     showing that pooling the left-cut and right-cut viewpoints isolates every
     sample point (discreteness), while their agreement keeps only two-sided
     neighbourhoods.

Self-contained: standard library only.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from fractions import Fraction
from itertools import combinations
from typing import FrozenSet, Iterable, List, Sequence, Set, Tuple

# A finite topology is represented as a set of open sets; each open set is a
# frozenset of points.
Point = int
OpenSet = FrozenSet[Point]
Topology = FrozenSet[OpenSet]


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Exact verification of the collapse identity  [x, b) cap (a, x] = {x}
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def half_open_right(x: Fraction, b: Fraction, grid: Sequence[Fraction]) -> Set[Fraction]:
    """Points of `grid` lying in the right half-open interval [x, b)."""
    return {p for p in grid if x <= p < b}


def half_open_left(a: Fraction, x: Fraction, grid: Sequence[Fraction]) -> Set[Fraction]:
    """Points of `grid` lying in the left half-open interval (a, x]."""
    return {p for p in grid if a < p <= x}


def verify_singleton_collapse(
    a: Fraction, x: Fraction, b: Fraction, grid: Sequence[Fraction]
) -> bool:
    """Check [x, b) cap (a, x] = {x} on a rational grid (requires a < x < b)."""
    assert a < x < b, "identity requires a < x < b"
    left = half_open_left(a, x, grid)
    right = half_open_right(x, b, grid)
    return left & right == {x}


def demo_singleton_collapse() -> None:
    print("=" * 70)
    print("1. SINGLETON COLLAPSE:  [x, b) cap (a, x] = {x}   (exact rationals)")
    print("=" * 70)
    # A dense rational grid on [-2, 2] with step 1/12.
    step = Fraction(1, 12)
    grid = [Fraction(-24) * step + k * step for k in range(0, 97)]
    triples = [
        (Fraction(-1), Fraction(0), Fraction(1)),
        (Fraction(-1, 2), Fraction(1, 3), Fraction(3, 2)),
        (Fraction(-2), Fraction(-1, 4), Fraction(1)),
        (Fraction(0), Fraction(1, 2), Fraction(2)),
    ]
    all_ok = True
    for (a, x, b) in triples:
        ok = verify_singleton_collapse(a, x, b, grid)
        all_ok &= ok
        print(f"  a={str(a):>6}  x={str(x):>6}  b={str(b):>6}  ->  "
              f"[x,b) cap (a,x] = {{{x}}}  : {ok}")
    print(f"\n  All singleton-collapse checks passed: {all_ok}\n")


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Finite lattice of topologies: consensus (sup) and possibility (inf)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def generate_topology(ground: FrozenSet[Point], subbasis: Iterable[OpenSet]) -> Topology:
    """Smallest topology on `ground` containing `subbasis`.

    Close the subbasis (together with empty set and the whole space) under
    finite intersections, then under arbitrary unions.
    """
    empty: OpenSet = frozenset()
    sub: Set[OpenSet] = {empty, ground}
    for s in subbasis:
        sub.add(frozenset(s) & ground)

    # Close under pairwise (hence finite) intersections.
    basis: Set[OpenSet] = set(sub)
    changed = True
    while changed:
        changed = False
        for u in list(basis):
            for v in list(basis):
                w = u & v
                if w not in basis:
                    basis.add(w)
                    changed = True

    # Close under arbitrary unions (build all unions of basis elements).
    opens: Set[OpenSet] = {empty}
    for r in range(1, len(basis) + 1):
        for combo in combinations(basis, r):
            union: OpenSet = frozenset().union(*combo)
            opens.add(union)
    opens.add(empty)
    opens.add(ground)
    return frozenset(opens)


def is_finer(t: Topology, s: Topology) -> bool:
    """t is finer than s  (t <= s in the refinement order):  every s-open is t-open."""
    return s <= t


def consensus(topologies: Sequence[Topology]) -> Topology:
    """Consensus (supremum): sets open in EVERY observer -> intersection of opens."""
    if not topologies:
        raise ValueError("need at least one topology")
    result: Set[OpenSet] = set(topologies[0])
    for t in topologies[1:]:
        result &= set(t)
    return frozenset(result)


def possibility(ground: FrozenSet[Point], topologies: Sequence[Topology]) -> Topology:
    """Possibility (infimum): topology GENERATED by the union of all observers' opens."""
    union_opens: Set[OpenSet] = set()
    for t in topologies:
        union_opens |= set(t)
    return generate_topology(ground, union_opens)


def discrete(ground: FrozenSet[Point]) -> Topology:
    pts = list(ground)
    opens: Set[OpenSet] = {frozenset()}
    for r in range(1, len(pts) + 1):
        for combo in combinations(pts, r):
            opens.add(frozenset(combo))
    return frozenset(opens)


def demo_lattice_duality() -> None:
    print("=" * 70)
    print("2. LATTICE DUALITY:  possibility <= observer <= consensus")
    print("=" * 70)
    ground: FrozenSet[Point] = frozenset({0, 1, 2})
    # Two genuinely disagreeing observers on {0,1,2}.
    obs_A = generate_topology(ground, [frozenset({0}), frozenset({0, 1})])
    obs_B = generate_topology(ground, [frozenset({2}), frozenset({1, 2})])

    con = consensus([obs_A, obs_B])
    pos = possibility(ground, [obs_A, obs_B])

    print(f"  |ground| = {len(ground)}   points = {sorted(ground)}")
    print(f"  observer A opens: {sorted(map(sorted, obs_A))}")
    print(f"  observer B opens: {sorted(map(sorted, obs_B))}")
    print(f"  consensus opens : {sorted(map(sorted, con))}")
    print(f"  possibility opens: {sorted(map(sorted, pos))}")

    # Sandwich: possibility finer than each observer; each observer finer than consensus.
    checks = {
        "possibility <= A": is_finer(pos, obs_A),
        "possibility <= B": is_finer(pos, obs_B),
        "A <= consensus": is_finer(obs_A, con),
        "B <= consensus": is_finer(obs_B, con),
        "possibility == discrete": pos == discrete(ground),
    }
    print()
    for name, ok in checks.items():
        print(f"    {name:>28} : {ok}")
    print()


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Half-open observers on a finite ordered sample of the line
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def right_looking_topology(sample: Sequence[Fraction]) -> Topology:
    """Lower-limit observer on a finite ordered sample: basic opens are the
    'right rays'  {p : p >= sample[i]} = [sample[i], +inf) restricted to the sample."""
    ground = frozenset(range(len(sample)))
    subbasis = [frozenset(j for j in range(len(sample)) if sample[j] >= sample[i])
                for i in range(len(sample))]
    return generate_topology(ground, subbasis)


def left_looking_topology(sample: Sequence[Fraction]) -> Topology:
    """Upper-limit observer: basic opens are the 'left rays'
    {p : p <= sample[i]} = (-inf, sample[i]] restricted to the sample."""
    ground = frozenset(range(len(sample)))
    subbasis = [frozenset(j for j in range(len(sample)) if sample[j] <= sample[i])
                for i in range(len(sample))]
    return generate_topology(ground, subbasis)


def demo_half_open_observers() -> None:
    print("=" * 70)
    print("3. HALF-OPEN OBSERVERS on a finite ordered sample of the line")
    print("=" * 70)
    sample: List[Fraction] = [Fraction(k, 2) for k in range(-2, 3)]  # -1, -1/2, 0, 1/2, 1
    print(f"  sample points: {[str(s) for s in sample]}")

    right = right_looking_topology(sample)   # left-cut viewpoint
    left = left_looking_topology(sample)     # right-cut viewpoint
    ground = frozenset(range(len(sample)))

    pos = possibility(ground, [left, right])
    con = consensus([left, right])

    # Each singleton = right-ray cap left-ray  (the finite analogue of [x,b) cap (a,x]).
    print("\n  Pooling the two viewpoints isolates every sample point:")
    for i, val in enumerate(sample):
        singleton = frozenset({i})
        print(f"    point {str(val):>5}  ->  {{{val}}} is possibility-open: "
              f"{singleton in pos}")

    print(f"\n  possibility == discrete : {pos == discrete(ground)}")
    print(f"  #consensus opens = {len(con)}  (agreement keeps far fewer opens)")
    print(f"  #possibility opens = {len(pos)} = 2^{len(sample)} "
          f"(every subset is open)\n")


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def main() -> None:
    demo_singleton_collapse()
    demo_lattice_duality()
    demo_half_open_observers()
    print("=" * 70)
    print("SUMMARY")
    print("=" * 70)
    print("  * Consensus of the two half-open observers reconstructs the")
    print("    two-sided (Euclidean) neighbourhoods.")
    print("  * Possibility of the SAME two observers collapses to the discrete")
    print("    topology via  [x, b) cap (a, x] = {x}.")
    print("  * One fixed pair of observers, two opposite realities.")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

algorithms.description: Constructs the smallest topology on a finite ground set containing a given subbasis. It first augments the subbasis with the empty set and the whole space, closes it under pairwise intersections to obtain a basis (a fixed-point loop), and finally forms all unions of basis elements. For a subbasis producing a basis of size m the intersection closure costs O(m^2) per pass over at most m passes, and the union closure enumerates up to 2^m combinations; it is exact and is the workhorse for computing both consensus and possibility on finite models.

Complexity is dominated by the generation step on the pooled subbasis.

algorithms.name: Possibility Number Search by Minimal Discretizing Subset
algorithms.description: Determines the possibility number: the least number of candidate coarser observers whose pooled possibility topology is discrete (every singleton open). It searches subsets by increasing size and tests discreteness of the pooled possibility, returning the first size that succeeds. Worst-case cost is exponential in the number of candidate observers (a subset search), but for the real-line twin observers it certifies the value two.

from itertools import combinations
from typing import FrozenSet, List, Sequence, Set

Point = int
OpenSet = FrozenSet[Point]
Topology = FrozenSet[OpenSet]


def is_discrete(ground: FrozenSet[Point], topology: Topology) -> bool:
    """True iff every singleton {p} is open (equivalently topology has 2**|ground| opens)."""
    return all(frozenset({p}) in topology for p in ground)


def possibility_number(ground: FrozenSet[Point],
                       candidate_observers: Sequence[Topology],
                       generate, possibility) -> int:
    """Least number of the given (coarser) observers whose pooled possibility is
    discrete. Searches by increasing subset size; returns -1 if none suffice.
    """
    n = len(candidate_observers)
    for k in range(1, n + 1):
        for combo in combinations(range(n), k):
            pooled = possibility(ground, [candidate_observers[i] for i in combo])
            if is_discrete(ground, pooled):
                return k
    return -1

future_directions:
# Future Directions

Five self-contained, falsifiable conjectures arising from the study of *possibility*
topologies (pooled resolution) as the order-dual of *consensus* topologies (unanimous
agreement) among a family of observers, each assigning their own topology to a fixed set.

## 1. The Possibility Number

Alongside the number of observers whose *agreement* reconstructs a space, define its dual:
the least number of coarser observers whose *pooled* view already isolates every point,
turning the space discrete. **Conjecture:** the real line has possibility number exactly
two — the left-looking and right-looking half-open viewpoints together isolate every point
through the collapse `[x, x+1) ∩ (x-1, x] = {x}`, and no single coarser observer isolates
anything — and a metrizable space has finite possibility number if and only if it carries a
countable network.

The key insight is that discreteness of the pooled topology is a *pointwise* condition:
each singleton must appear as a finite intersection of open sets contributed by individual
observers, so the possibility number measures how many viewpoints must be superimposed
before every point becomes individually distinguishable.

Why now? The exact discreteness collapse of the two half-open viewpoints on the line has
just been established, giving a concrete anchor case from which the general invariant can be
calibrated and tested against classical spaces.

## 2. Join-Reducibility Governs Genuine Representability

Whether a space can be reconstructed as the agreement of two strictly sharper viewpoints is
equivalent to whether its topology is a join of two strictly smaller topologies in the
lattice of all topologies on the set. **Conjecture:** the viewpoints that *cannot* be split
this way are exactly the discrete topology together with those whose lattice of open sets
has a unique maximal proper element, and on a finite set they are precisely the topologies
whose specialisation order is a forest with a single source.

The key insight is that "how many observers reconstruct a space" is not a geometric
question at all but an order-theoretic one about covers and atoms in the lattice of
topologies, so rigidity is a statement about join-irreducibility rather than about the
space's shape.

Why now? The reduction of representability to a single join-reducibility condition is in
hand, so the classification of the rigid (unsplittable) viewpoints becomes a concrete and
attackable lattice problem.

## 3. Separation and Phantom Number Are Independent

Being highly separated (metrizable, Hausdorff) neither forces nor forbids a low observer
count: the blurred two-point space needs only two observers, while the fully-resolved
two-point space — as separated as possible — cannot be split at all. **Conjecture:** for any
target observer count in {zero, two, infinite} and any consistent combination of the
classical separation axioms, there is a space realising exactly that count and exactly those
axioms.

The key insight is that separation strength and observer count are orthogonal invariants:
one measures how well points can be told apart within a single topology, the other measures
how a topology decomposes across a family of observers, and the two can be dialed
independently.

"""
Phantom Topologies: Spaces That Change When You Look at Them
===========================================================

Numerical demonstrations of the two headline results about observer-dependent
("phantom") topologies on the real line:

  * CONSENSUS RECONSTRUCTION.  The Euclidean topology on R is the *agreement*
    (supremum in the lattice of topologies) of two complementary observers:
    the lower-limit / right-looking observer (basic opens  [x, b) ) and the
    upper-limit / left-looking observer (basic opens  (a, x] ).  A set is
    Euclidean-open iff it is open for BOTH observers.

  * POSSIBILITY COLLAPSE.  The *possibility* (infimum) of the SAME two
    observers is the DISCRETE topology, because for a < x < b

            [x, b)  cap  (a, x]  =  {x}.

    Every singleton becomes open, hence every set is open.

Because R is infinite, we illustrate the phenomena three ways:

  1. Exact rational verification of the singleton-collapse identity
     [x, b) cap (a, x] = {x}  on dense rational grids (no floating point).
  2. A finite lattice-of-topologies engine that computes consensus (supremum)
     and possibility (infimum) of arbitrary finite topologies, confirming the
     sandwich  possibility <= observer <= consensus  and the modal duality.
  3. A "half-open observers" model on a finite ordered sample of the line,
     showing that pooling the left-cut and right-cut viewpoints isolates every
     sample point (discreteness), while their agreement keeps only two-sided
     neighbourhoods.

Self-contained: standard library only.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from fractions import Fraction
from itertools import combinations
from typing import FrozenSet, Iterable, List, Sequence, Set, Tuple

# A finite topology is represented as a set of open sets; each open set is a
# frozenset of points.
Point = int
OpenSet = FrozenSet[Point]
Topology = FrozenSet[OpenSet]


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Exact verification of the collapse identity  [x, b) cap (a, x] = {x}
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def half_open_right(x: Fraction, b: Fraction, grid: Sequence[Fraction]) -> Set[Fraction]:
    """Points of `grid` lying in the right half-open interval [x, b)."""
    return {p for p in grid if x <= p < b}


def half_open_left(a: Fraction, x: Fraction, grid: Sequence[Fraction]) -> Set[Fraction]:
    """Points of `grid` lying in the left half-open interval (a, x]."""
    return {p for p in grid if a < p <= x}


def verify_singleton_collapse(
    a: Fraction, x: Fraction, b: Fraction, grid: Sequence[Fraction]
) -> bool:
    """Check [x, b) cap (a, x] = {x} on a rational grid (requires a < x < b)."""
    assert a < x < b, "identity requires a < x < b"
    left = half_open_left(a, x, grid)
    right = half_open_right(x, b, grid)
    return left & right == {x}


def demo_singleton_collapse() -> None:
    print("=" * 70)
    print("1. SINGLETON COLLAPSE:  [x, b) cap (a, x] = {x}   (exact rationals)")
    print("=" * 70)
    # A dense rational grid on [-2, 2] with step 1/12.
    step = Fraction(1, 12)
    grid = [Fraction(-24) * step + k * step for k in range(0, 97)]
    triples = [
        (Fraction(-1), Fraction(0), Fraction(1)),
        (Fraction(-1, 2), Fraction(1, 3), Fraction(3, 2)),
        (Fraction(-2), Fraction(-1, 4), Fraction(1)),
        (Fraction(0), Fraction(1, 2), Fraction(2)),
    ]
    all_ok = True
    for (a, x, b) in triples:
        ok = verify_singleton_collapse(a, x, b, grid)
        all_ok &= ok
        print(f"  a={str(a):>6}  x={str(x):>6}  b={str(b):>6}  ->  "
              f"[x,b) cap (a,x] = {{{x}}}  : {ok}")
    print(f"\n  All singleton-collapse checks passed: {all_ok}\n")


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Finite lattice of topologies: consensus (sup) and possibility (inf)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def generate_topology(ground: FrozenSet[Point], subbasis: Iterable[OpenSet]) -> Topology:
    """Smallest topology on `ground` containing `subbasis`.

    Close the subbasis (together with empty set and the whole space) under
    finite intersections, then under arbitrary unions.
    """
    empty: OpenSet = frozenset()
    sub: Set[OpenSet] = {empty, ground}
    for s in subbasis:
        sub.add(frozenset(s) & ground)

    # Close under pairwise (hence finite) intersections.
    basis: Set[OpenSet] = set(sub)
    changed = True
    while changed:
        changed = False
        for u in list(basis):
            for v in list(basis):
                w = u & v
                if w not in basis:
                    basis.add(w)
                    changed = True

    # Close under arbitrary unions (build all unions of basis elements).
    opens: Set[OpenSet] = {empty}
    for r in range(1, len(basis) + 1):
        for combo in combinations(basis, r):
            union: OpenSet = frozenset().union(*combo)
            opens.add(union)
    opens.add(empty)
    opens.add(ground)
    return frozenset(opens)


def is_finer(t: Topology, s: Topology) -> bool:
    """t is finer than s  (t <= s in the refinement order):  every s-open is t-open."""
    return s <= t


def consensus(topologies: Sequence[Topology]) -> Topology:
    """Consensus (supremum): sets open in EVERY observer -> intersection of opens."""
    if not topologies:
        raise ValueError("need at least one topology")
    result: Set[OpenSet] = set(topologies[0])
    for t in topologies[1:]:
        result &= set(t)
    return frozenset(result)


def possibility(ground: FrozenSet[Point], topologies: Sequence[Topology]) -> Topology:
    """Possibility (infimum): topology GENERATED by the union of all observers' opens."""
    union_opens: Set[OpenSet] = set()
    for t in topologies:
        union_opens |= set(t)
    return generate_topology(ground, union_opens)


def discrete(ground: FrozenSet[Point]) -> Topology:
    pts = list(ground)
    opens: Set[OpenSet] = {frozenset()}
    for r in range(1, len(pts) + 1):
        for combo in combinations(pts, r):
            opens.add(frozenset(combo))
    return frozenset(opens)


def demo_lattice_duality() -> None:
    print("=" * 70)
    print("2. LATTICE DUALITY:  possibility <= observer <= consensus")
    print("=" * 70)
    ground: FrozenSet[Point] = frozenset({0, 1, 2})
    # Two genuinely disagreeing observers on {0,1,2}.
    obs_A = generate_topology(ground, [frozenset({0}), frozenset({0, 1})])
    obs_B = generate_topology(ground, [frozenset({2}), frozenset({1, 2})])

    con = consensus([obs_A, obs_B])
    pos = possibility(ground, [obs_A, obs_B])

    print(f"  |ground| = {len(ground)}   points = {sorted(ground)}")
    print(f"  observer A opens: {sorted(map(sorted, obs_A))}")
    print(f"  observer B opens: {sorted(map(sorted, obs_B))}")
    print(f"  consensus opens : {sorted(map(sorted, con))}")
    print(f"  possibility opens: {sorted(map(sorted, pos))}")

    # Sandwich: possibility finer than each observer; each observer finer than consensus.
    checks = {
        "possibility <= A": is_finer(pos, obs_A),
        "possibility <= B": is_finer(pos, obs_B),
        "A <= consensus": is_finer(obs_A, con),
        "B <= consensus": is_finer(obs_B, con),
        "possibility == discrete": pos == discrete(ground),
    }
    print()
    for name, ok in checks.items():
        print(f"    {name:>28} : {ok}")
    print()


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Half-open observers on a finite ordered sample of the line

def right_looking_topology(sample: Sequence[Fraction]) -> Topology:
    """Lower-limit observer on a finite ordered sample: basic opens are the
    'right rays'  {p : p >= sample[i]} = [sample[i], +inf) restricted to the sample."""
    ground = frozenset(range(len(sample)))
    subbasis = [frozenset(j for j in range(len(sample)) if sample[j] >= sample[i])
                for i in range(len(sample))]
    return generate_topology(ground, subbasis)


def left_looking_topology(sample: Sequence[Fraction]) -> Topology:
    """Upper-limit observer: basic opens are the 'left rays'
    {p : p <= sample[i]} = (-inf, sample[i]] restricted to the sample."""
    ground = frozenset(range(len(sample)))
    subbasis = [frozenset(j for j in range(len(sample)) if sample[j] <= sample[i])
                for i in range(len(sample))]
    return generate_topology(ground, subbasis)


def demo_half_open_observers() -> None:
    print("=" * 70)
    print("3. HALF-OPEN OBSERVERS on a finite ordered sample of the line")
    print("=" * 70)
    sample: List[Fraction] = [Fraction(k, 2) for k in range(-2, 3)]  # -1, -1/2, 0, 1/2, 1
    print(f"  sample points: {[str(s) for s in sample]}")

    right = right_looking_topology(sample)   # left-cut viewpoint
    left = left_looking_topology(sample)     # right-cut viewpoint
    ground = frozenset(range(len(sample)))

    pos = possibility(ground, [left, right])
    con = consensus([left, right])

    # Each singleton = right-ray cap left-ray  (the finite analogue of [x,b) cap (a,x]).
    print("\n  Pooling the two viewpoints isolates every sample point:")
    for i, val in enumerate(sample):
        singleton = frozenset({i})
        print(f"    point {str(val):>5}  ->  {{{val}}} is possibility-open: "
              f"{singleton in pos}")

    print(f"\n  possibility == discrete : {pos == discrete(ground)}")
    print(f"  #consensus opens = {len(con)}  (agreement keeps far fewer opens)")
    print(f"  #possibility opens = {len(pos)} = 2^{len(sample)} "
          f"(every subset is open)\n")
